# Source text
Article 22, Civil Code, as quoted in BDO Unibank, Inc. v. Barcellano, G.R. No. 261264, February 12, 2026: "Every person who through an act of performance by another, or any other means, acquires or comes into possession of something at the expense of the latter without just or legal ground, shall return the same to him."

Article 2154, Civil Code, as quoted in the same case: "If something is received when there is no right to demand it, and it was unduly delivered through mistake, the obligation to return it arises."

In BDO Unibank, Inc. v. Barcellano, G.R. No. 261264, February 12, 2026, the Court said: "In handling their transactions, banks are required to exercise extraordinary diligence, which is more than that of a Roman pater familias or a good father of a family."

In BDO Unibank, Inc. v. Barcellano, G.R. No. 261264, February 12, 2026, the Court also said: "Before the check is cleared for deposit, the collecting bank can only assume at its own risk that the check will be cleared and paid out."

# Key points for the tutor (reviewer-approved)
- Banks are imbued with public interest. In handling their transactions they must exercise extraordinary diligence, which is more than the diligence of a good father of a family.
- A bank that pays out on a check before it is cleared with the drawee bank departs from ordinary banking practice. In that situation the collecting bank assumes the risk of non-payment.
- In BDO Unibank, Inc. v. Barcellano, G.R. No. 261264, February 12, 2026, the Court found gross negligence on three grounds: the bank credited the check before clearing it, the teller wrongly treated a regional check as a local one, and the bank did not detect the error until the check came back under a stop payment order. The Court held that the bank's own negligence was the proximate cause of its loss.
- Solutio indebiti (Art. 2154) requires payment made through mistake, with no binding relation between payor and recipient. The Court approved the view that a bank's failure to follow its own duty of extraordinary diligence is not the kind of "mistake" that gives rise to the obligation to return, and that no recovery is due when the mistake is one of gross negligence.
- Unjust enrichment (Art. 22) requires a benefit without valid basis and at another's expense. The claimant must clearly show that the other party knowingly received a benefit to which it was not entitled.
- The bank did not prove that the depositor knew why the check was stopped. She even tried to withdraw the remaining balance, so the Court inferred that she believed in good faith that the money was hers. No unjust enrichment and no constructive trust followed.
- Procedural note: an acquittal in the estafa case barred civil liability arising from the crime. The Court still examined whether liability could rest on another source of obligation, and found none.

# Recitation drill: application fact pattern
Scenario: Lorna deposits a check drawn on a provincial branch of another bank into her account at Metro Savers Bank. The Metro Savers teller wrongly tags it for the shorter local clearing period, even though the drawee branch is printed on the check, and the money becomes available. Lorna withdraws part of it. Days later the check is returned under a stop payment order. The bank demands that Lorna return the amount under solutio indebiti and unjust enrichment, but it cannot show that she knew why the check was stopped.
Model answer: The bank cannot recover. Under BDO Unibank, Inc. v. Barcellano, G.R. No. 261264, February 12, 2026, banks must exercise extraordinary diligence. A bank that releases funds on an uncleared check assumes the risk of non-payment. The teller's mistake was gross negligence, not the kind of mistake that triggers Art. 2154. Art. 22 also fails because the bank did not show that Lorna knowingly received money she was not entitled to.

# Problem drill: exam or bar-style problem
Problem: (Original problem based on BDO Unibank, Inc. v. Barcellano, G.R. No. 261264, February 12, 2026. Past Bar years: reviewer to confirm.) Ernesto owns a hardware store in Tarlac. A customer pays him with a check drawn on a bank branch in Davao, and Ernesto deposits it to his savings account at Pampanga Trust Bank late in the afternoon. The branch teller processes it under the shorter local clearing period even though the Davao drawee branch is clearly printed on the check. The bank credits the amount and Ernesto withdraws part of it to pay suppliers. Four days later the check is returned because the drawer issued a stop payment order. Ernesto does not know the reason for the stop payment order. The bank demands that he return the withdrawn amount, invoking Article 22 (unjust enrichment) and Article 2154 (solutio indebiti) of the Civil Code, and alleging that the crediting was a mere mistake. Ernesto refuses. Is Ernesto bound to return the amount?
Model answer:
(Answer) No. Ernesto is not bound to return the amount on the grounds the bank invokes. The bank's loss was caused by its own gross negligence, and it cannot show unjust enrichment or a payment by mistake that gives rise to the obligation to return.

(Legal basis) Banks are imbued with public interest and must exercise extraordinary diligence in their transactions. Paying out on a check before it is cleared with the drawee bank is contrary to ordinary banking practice, and the collecting bank assumes the risk. Article 2154 of the Civil Code applies only when something is unduly delivered through mistake, and no recovery is due if the mistake is one of gross negligence. Article 22 requires a benefit without just or legal ground, and the claimant must clearly show that the recipient knowingly received a benefit to which it was not entitled. These rules are applied in BDO Unibank, Inc. v. Barcellano, G.R. No. 261264, February 12, 2026.

(Application) The teller treated a regional check as a local one although the Davao drawee branch was plainly visible on its face. The bank also credited the amount and allowed withdrawal before clearance, and it found out only when the check came back. As in Barcellano, these are acts of gross negligence and the proximate cause of the loss. They are not an excusable mistake of fact or law under Article 2154. The bank also did not show that Ernesto knew the reason for the stop payment order or knew he was not entitled to the funds. He deposited the check in the ordinary course of business and withdrew funds that the bank itself had made available, so there is no showing that he knowingly retained an undeserved benefit.

(Conclusion) Ernesto is not obliged to return the amount under Article 22 or Article 2154. Pampanga Trust Bank bears the loss caused by its own failure to exercise extraordinary diligence.

# Objective and multiple-choice quiz (Year 1-2)
Q (multiple choice): Under BDO Unibank, Inc. v. Barcellano, G.R. No. 261264, February 12, 2026, what is the standard of diligence required of a bank in handling its transactions?
A) Ordinary diligence of a good father of a family
B) Extraordinary diligence, more than that of a good father of a family
C) Slight care only, since the depositor also has duties
D) No fixed standard, because banks are private entities
Correct: B
Hint: The Court stressed that the banking business is imbued with public interest.
Hint: The standard is higher than that of a Roman pater familias.
Why: The Court held that banks must exercise extraordinary diligence, more than that of a good father of a family. Its failure to do so was gross negligence.

Q (multiple choice): A collecting bank credits a regional check as if it were a local check, and the depositor withdraws part of the amount before the check is dishonored. The bank's loss is attributed to its own gross negligence. May the bank recover the amount from the depositor under solutio indebiti?
A) Yes, because any payment not due must be returned
B) Yes, because the depositor withdrew before clearance
C) No, because the payment was not made through the kind of mistake Art. 2154 contemplates, and no recovery is due when the mistake is gross negligence
D) No, but only if the depositor is a bank employee
Correct: C
Hint: Art. 2154 requires that the thing was unduly delivered through mistake.
Hint: The Court approved the view that a bank's failure to exercise extraordinary diligence is not such a mistake.
Why: In BDO Unibank, Inc. v. Barcellano, G.R. No. 261264, February 12, 2026, the Court held that solutio indebiti did not apply. The error came from the bank's gross negligence, and the bank did not show that the depositor knowingly received something she was not entitled to.

Q (objective): Who bears the risk when a collecting bank pays out on a check before it is cleared with the drawee bank?
Accept: the collecting bank | the bank | the collecting bank assumes the risk
Hint: The Court said the bank can only assume that the check will be cleared "at its own risk."
Why: Under BDO Unibank, Inc. v. Barcellano, G.R. No. 261264, February 12, 2026, paying out before clearance is contrary to ordinary banking practice, and the collecting bank bears the risk of non-payment.

Q (objective): Name the Civil Code article on unjust enrichment that the bank invoked, and the article on solutio indebiti, in BDO Unibank, Inc. v. Barcellano, G.R. No. 261264, February 12, 2026.
Accept: Article 22 and Article 2154 | Art. 22 and Art. 2154 | 22 and 2154
Hint: One is in the Preliminary Title on Human Relations. The other is in the chapter on quasi-contracts.
Why: Article 22 requires a benefit without just or legal ground at another's expense. Article 2154 requires something received without right to demand it and delivered through mistake. The Court found neither satisfied.
